description: Buildings and homes in the Netherlands must get rid of natural gas. Collective heat will play an important role in this - in addition to heat pumps and sustainable gas. There is a lot of potential for making the built environment more sustainable in collective heat systems, for three reasons: 51 1. collective heat systems are socially the cheapest option for certain neighbourhoods (e.g. where homes are built close to each other and insulation is limited), 2. collective heat systems play an important role in the energy system to unlock certain sustainable sources that otherwise remain unused (e.g. geothermal, aquathermal and residual heat) and 3. collective heat systems limit the necessary reinforcement of the electricity grid for the districts concerned. Over the last few years, projects in a number of major cities have faced barriers to affordability, putting them on hold. For each project, stakeholders look at what is possible to bring these collective heat projects further. However, it also requires longer-term measures to make collective heat attractive to end-users. Last year, first steps were taken to improve this, both through earlier legislative pathways and through additional policy measures. New legislation is discussed below: the Municipal Instruments Heat Transition Act (Wgiw) and the Collective Heat Act (Wcw). These two laws create a robust framework that boosts the development of affordable collective heat. In addition to this legislation, additional instruments are being developed to strengthen the public implementing power, such as a Heat Networks Guarantee Scheme (GRW). € 174.5 million will be made available from the Climate Fund to the Guarantee Scheme for Heat Grids (GRW). This amount will be used in particular as a risk provision in the budget. The risk scheme shall be drawn up at the earliest from mid-2026 for a period of 5 years after which the scheme shall be evaluated.52 As of 2023, the Heat Networks Investment Subsidy (WIS) has been introduced (see also below), which helps to reduce the unprofitable top by means of an investment subsidy. After each opening, the scheme is evaluated, taking into account the lessons learned from 2023 to improve the scheme. A user who connects to a heat network will have to deal with connection costs and internal adjustments. This is discussed in the section on subsidies for connection costs for in-house adjustments. The necessary scaling-up of renewable sources for heat networks is stimulated through the SDE++ (which is addressed in this chapter under ‘Tackling renewable energy sources’), with its own ‘gates’ for low- and high-temperature heat projects.

The Collective Heat Act (Wcw) will replace the Heat Act. Since 2014, the Heat Act has regulated the supply of heat to consumers and small and medium-sized enterprises for connections up to 100 kilowatts. The Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM) oversees the implementation of the Heat Act. The Wcw aims to facilitate the growth and sustainability of collective heat systems in the built environment. Municipalities will be given guidance to implement their management role in making the built environment more sustainable, as agreed in the Climate Agreement. Sustainability standards are included that drive the efficient sustainability of the heat supply. Security of supply and consumer protection are better ensured, and where possible aligned with the protection at E&G. Finally, new tariff rules are introduced, which increase transparency and gradually base heat tariffs on the actual costs incurred, instead of the current gas reference. With this, the bill steers towards fairer heat rates for consumers and clear revenues for heat companies. A transition period of ten years is foreseen, whereby heat networks must be in public hands for more than 50 percent by 2036. On July 3rd, the bill was passed by the House of Representatives. On 9 December, the Senate approved the Collective Heat Act (Wcw).

The Heat Networks Investment Grant (WIS) is a multi-year opening for cumulative € 1.6 billion from the Climate Fund and aims to stimulate the realization of heat networks by lowering the unprofitable top. The WIS has been opened twice so far, for the first time in 2023 and for the second time in 2024. A total of 14 projects have been completed and 6 applications are still pending. In 2024, only a quarter of the total open budget was requested and the remaining budget was advanced. The disappointing enthusiasm is due to the reluctance of the large private heat companies to invest in new projects, pending clarification about the public market organisation of the bill Collective Heat Act. The original target for 2030 (500,000 new connections in the existing construction compared to 2021) is no longer realistic and has therefore recently been adjusted to 200,000 new connections in 2030 .

New Heat Now! (NWN) is an incentive programme of the Dutch government that was established under the National Growth Fund. The program aims to accelerate the development and realization of sustainable collective heat projects. In particular, NWN focuses on projects that use residual heat, aquathermal energy, geothermal energy and other renewable sources. The aim is to enable natural gas-free heating, especially in urban areas, and thus make an important contribution to the energy transition. Since its launch, NWN has made significant progress in realizing natural gas-free neighborhoods and promoting innovative heat solutions. The implementation of NWN projects is supported by grants and guidance, with the focus on combining different heat sources and optimising existing infrastructure. In addition, work is being done to strengthen the direction and cooperation between public and private parties, with the aim of building a robust and future-proof heat infrastructure. The total amount of New Heat Now! is €200 million. Of this, almost €160 million has already been committed to projects, of which €25 million has already been disbursed. The projects consist of 10 ‘flywheel projects’ (warmtenet projects) and 5 innovation projects (warmtenet related) which are united in the Leer & Development Programme of New Heat Now!. Within the L&O, bottlenecks and solutions are brought to the table and discussed openly. Through the joint efforts of municipalities, housing corporations, heat companies and residents, 52 Letter to Parliament on the topicalisation of collective heat | Parliamentary Paper | Rijksoverheid.nl sustainable heat solutions are realized that contribute to the energy transition and the achievement of climate objectives. Together with the WIS scheme, the programme contributes to a future-proof, sustainable heat supply.

measure_name: Subsidies for connection costs for in-house adjustments
description: A user who connects to a heat network will have to deal with connection costs and internal adjustments. In order to reduce these costs, various subsidies are available. These are components for heat networks from the current broader schemes ISDE (homeowners), DUMAVA (social real estate) and SVVE (for VvEs). In addition, the incentive scheme for natural gas-free rental housing (SAH) is specifically available for the costs incurred for the connection of existing rental housing and owner-occupied housing with purchase and rental housing (or mixed owner-occupied housing) to an external heat network. The commitment is that a new or adapted scheme will enter into force in 2026, streamlining these schemes.

measure_name: Incentive scheme for natural gas-free rental housing (SAH)
description: The Stimulation Scheme for natural gas-free rental housing (SAH) is a subsidy for landlords (housing corporations, institutional investors and private landlords) and mixed VvEs that offers a chance for contributions for the connection of existing (rental) homes to an external heat network. The SAH was part of the Startmotor approach of the climate agreement, aimed at a first scale-up of the sustainability of the housing stock by connecting 100,000 homes to heat in the short term. With the SAH, VvEs and landlords receive subsidies for existing homes that go off natural gas within 6 years through a connection to a heat network. There is a subsidy for adjustments in the homes (indoor housing costs), the connection costs to a heat network and the purchase of fixed income. If the houses are already connected to a heat network, but natural gas is still used for hot water and / or for cooking, you can also apply for SAH for the indoor costs. The rental property will then no longer use natural gas after the execution. From 2025 onwards, subsidies will be available for the purchase of the fixed-duty costs for heat supply for landlords. They must fully use this to buy off the fixed costs for a heat network for ten years, so that the costs of the tenant will ultimately be lower. A maximum of 8000 euros can be requested per property. The total budget for 2024 was €200 million. As of 2025, the budget has been increased by 25 million, intended for a fixed contribution of €2,000 per house for the purchase of fixed income.

The sustainability of collective heat sources is one of the objectives of the Collective Heat Act (Wcw). The Wcw will require heat companies to gradually increase their sustainability towards 0 kg of CO₂ equivalent emissions by 2050. This is done by setting a sustainability standard per heat lot that regulates the maximum emissions of greenhouse gases. There will be a gradual phasing-out path for the permitted emissions per year that will be elaborated in lower regulations. Once every five years, the established standards will be evaluated for effectiveness and impact. The Wcw also regulates that the Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM) supervises and can impose sanctions if the permitted emissions are violated. From five years after the first exceedance of the standard, the ACM can firmly maintain and, in the event of a persistent violation, advise the municipality to withdraw the designation or exemption of the heating company. In exceptional cases, an exemption and extension of the performance standards can be granted by the ACM if sustainability is (temporarily) not feasible. Exemption from sustainability standards can be granted in case a heat company cannot meet these standards because the realisation of a new sustainable heat source is not feasible. The Wcw also stipulates that heat companies must share their emissions reports. ACM will publish the performance annually and consumers should also receive the information on emissions via their invoices. Under the current Heat Act, since 2020, permit holders of heat networks have been obliged to report on the sustainability of the heat supplied in their management report. Permit holders are heat companies that supply heat to more than 10 customers simultaneously and 10,000 gigajoules or more per year. In 2024/25, a bill for the Heat Act is in preparation for the implementation of the EED. With this, the Heat Act is adapted to steer towards a more efficient grid or sustainability plans for this in the event of construction and major renovation. Municipal Instruments for Heat Transition Act (Wgiw) The Municipal Instruments for Heat Transition Act (Wgiw) contains amendments to the Environment Act and the Gas Act/Energy Act. The law gives municipalities the power to draw up local rules for the heat transition from gas to sustainable alternatives such as a heat pump or a heat network. Under the Wgiw, municipalities can order network operators to close off districts designated in the environmental plan from the gas. The law is therefore the final piece of the neighbourhood-oriented approach. The law aims to give municipalities the tools to designate areas within their municipality that, in the long term, will no longer be allowed to use fossil fuels for heating buildings and will switch to a sustainable heat supply. With this power, the municipality can implement the transition from natural gas to sustainable alternatives in the built environment by setting local rules. To this end, the municipality can designate districts in the environmental plan where an energy supply with renewable energy becomes available to replace natural gas, the so-called designation authority. The Wgiw requires municipalities to draw up a heat programme by 2026 at the latest. Among other things, the substantive requirements that that program must meet and the update obligation (of 5 years) are elaborated in a General Measure of Management (AMvB), called the Decree municipal instruments heat transition. In addition, various safeguards when deploying the power under the Wgiw are elaborated in the Bgiw. The Wgiw was adopted by the House of Representatives on 23 April 2024. The Senate adopted the proposal on 10 December 2024.53 The Bgiw was suspended from both the First and Second Chambers at the beginning of July (pending procedure). The aim is to have the full Wgiw and the Bgiw enter into force on 1 July 2026. Article IIA entered into force on 1 January. This concerns the amendments to the Heat Act in anticipation of the bill on collective heat that is now before the House of Representatives.

The heat program is the first step in the planning process under the Wgiw. In the Dutch Climate Agreement (2019), it was agreed that municipalities make plans (transition visions of heat) in which they make clear in which districts they will work in the next 10 years. The Wgiw stipulates that the transition vision heat will be applied as a mandatory program under the Environment and Planning Act, called the heat program. The heat program must be updated every 5 years. The heat programme indicates which districts the municipality will work with in the coming period, of at least ten years. This can involve both (the municipality's commitment to) insulation and the switch to a sustainable alternative to natural gas. This gives the municipality and stakeholders a picture of the heat transition in the built environment and gives them a perspective for action. The heat program describes whether, when and how the district is preserved. In doing so, the timeline of making the district more sustainable and potentially available sustainable heat alternatives are mapped out. By 31 December 2027, municipalities must update their current heat transition vision and adopt a new heat programme. Municipalities can make use of the knowledge and insights of the National Local Heat Transition Programme, including the heat programme support offer, when drawing up the heat programme.

measure_name: National Program for Local Heat Transition (NPLW)
description: The National Program Local Heat Transition (NPLW) is an inter-administrative program of the government, VNG and IPO. The NPLW was officially launched on 1 January 2023 and builds on the knowledge of the Natural Gas- Free Neighbourhoods Programme (PAW) and the Expertise Centre for Heat (ECW).

measure_name: Scheme for the capacity of local and regional authorities for climate and energy policy (CDOKE)
description: On 27 February 2023, the temporary scheme for the capacity of local and regional authorities for climate and energy policy (CDOKE) was published55. The aim of this scheme is to have municipalities and provinces build up an internal organisation aimed at carrying out tasks resulting from the Climate Agreement. The scheme initially allocated funds for three years. The recent recalibration of the scheme updates the activities and associated resources for the performance of the tasks for the period 2025-2030. In addition, the Regional Structure Grant Scheme National Programme for Local Heat Transition has been set56 up, with which municipalities can organise support at regional level with each other and with the help of the province and NPLW.

measure_name: National Insulation Programme (NIP): the local approach by municipalities
description: The local approach to isolation by municipalities concerns action line 1 of the National Insulation Programme57. The objective of action line 1 of the NIP is to isolate approximately 750,000 owner-occupied and mixed housing units between 2022 and 2030 through a local approach together with municipalities. Municipalities can submit multi-year plans aimed at improving homes with the worst energy labels and low WOZ values. For the local approach can be connected to the transition visions heat and residents initiatives. In this way, different channels reinforce each other as much as possible. Around €1.6 billion is currently available for Action Line 1. The funds can be used by municipalities to improve owner-occupied homes or homes in a mixed housing estate with energy label D or lower (or a similar energetic state) and 80% of the homes must have a WOZ value below the average of the WOZ value of owner-occupied homes in the municipality or below the NHG limit. These resources can be used for the application of insulation and ventilation measures, for financial support, but also for practical support in the sustainability process and relief. The funds can be used on top of national subsidies and are mainly intended to help people who need extra help the most to combat energy poverty as much as possible and to stimulate collective action. In all tranches of the local approach, the funds can also be used for do-it-yourself measures. Do-it-yourself can save costs when insulating. It also reduces the pressure on the execution capacity available in the market. The local approach builds on the resources already made available to municipalities between 2019 and 2023 that allowed small measures to be taken (such as the application of LED lamps, radiator foil and draft strips). With the approaches that have been developed for this purpose, networks have emerged and energy coaches and fixers have come ‘behind the front door’. From the networks, the contacts already made and the application of small measures, steps can also be taken to apply large measures.

measure_name: Green in and around the city
description: Urban green space is important for a livable city, for various functions. The Netherlands is working on the implementation of the EU Nature Restoration Regulation. In the coming period, an elaboration will be given to the article that focuses on urban ecosystems and within them urban green space and urban tree canopy cover. Building on the approach Green in and around the city (GIOS) of VRO and LVVN. With the GIOS Handreiking, we offer municipalities and provinces both substantive and process-based tools to include green equivalent to other themes within the spatial domain in planning. In the Handreiking we present a guarantee system. Municipalities and provinces can work directly, on a voluntary basis.

measure_name: The National Living and Safety Programme (NPLV)
description: The National Programme for Liveability and Safety (NPLV) works in 20 areas in Dutch cities to improve quality of life and safety, because it is under heavy pressure there. Three substantive goals are being worked on: improving poor housing and ensuring more mixed neighbourhoods, allowing residents to participate more in society and tackling (youth) crime. In the 20 NPLV areas, the construction of approximately 15,000 homes is in preparation with the use of the Housing Impulse (Wbi) and the Startbouwimpuls (Sbi). With the use of funds from the Housing Fund (VHF), almost 1,400 vulnerable homes have been improved, with 4,590 homes starting with this. Furthermore, a total of around 30,000 to 40,000 households in the NPLV areas have been helped with energy-saving facilities for lower energy bills and a healthier living environment. In five areas, 400 homes with energy label D-G have been insulated in the past year with the help of the National Insulation Programme (NIP).

measure_name: Approach aimed at individual homeowners, VvEs and rental properties

description: Owner-residents of owner-occupied homes are encouraged to get started with sustainability through attractive, widely accessible subsidies and financing. These are explained below. Furthermore, homeowners are encouraged and supported with communication campaigns, the national platform www.verbeterjehuis.nl and energy counters. These are also described later, in the section on Energiehuizen.

Action lines 1 and 3 of the National Insulation Programme are important pillars of the policy aimed at making owner-occupied homes more sustainable. Action Line 3 aims to isolate 750,000 owner-occupied homes on its own initiative (and through collective purchasing) by 2030. Action line 1 also provides additional support through municipalities for some 750,000 owner-occupiers who need it to become more sustainable (see above).

measure_name: Investment subsidy Sustainable Energy and Energy Savings (ISDE)
description: The Investment Grant for Sustainable Energy and Energy Saving (ISDE) is a subsidy for energy-saving and sustainable measures for homeowners and business users. The ISDE subsidizes on average 30% of the purchase costs. For insulation measures, 1 measure has a subsidy intensity of 15% and for 2 or more measures this is doubled to 30%. This is to encourage homeowners to take several measures at the same time. By 2026, the ISDE budget will be €500 million. Every year a new budget is available. ISDE will continue until 2030. A total of €2.25 billion is available for the period 2026 to 2030. Homeowners receive subsidies for: • insulation measures • heat pumps • solar water heaters • connection to the heat network • Electric Cooking Equipment Business users receive subsidies for: • heat pumps • solar water heaters • small-scale wind turbines It is also possible to apply for ISDE as an intermediary for a homeowner. In addition, since February 2024, municipalities can apply for and receive the ISDE on behalf of homeowners, in order to unburden their residents. Municipalities can thus pre-finance this part of the costs, for example with funds from the Specific Allowance (SpUk) Local Approach Isolation and subsequently submit and receive the application for the ISDE. As of 2024, a bonus subsidy will also be available if biobased environmentally friendly insulation material is used, as is the case with the Subsidy Scheme for Sustainability for Owners' Associations (SVVE) and the Subsidy Scheme for Sustainability and Maintenance of Rental Homes (SVOH). In addition, the subsidy conditions for monuments have been relaxed as of 2024.

measure_name: Insulation homes Groningen and North Drenthe
description: From 2025, homeowners in the province of Groningen and in the municipalities of Aa and Hunze, Noordenveld and Tynaarlo in North Drenthe can apply for a subsidy to isolate their home. This measure is one of the measures from the Cabinet response Nij Begun, following the report of the Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry into Natural Gas Extraction Groningen. The budget for measure 29 (Insulation approach for homes in Groningen and North Drenthe) is 1.65 billion euros. Of this, 1.5 billion is for measures and 150 million for implementation. The budget for measure 28 (Reinforcing and combining insulating measures) is EUR 380 million. Different conditions apply depending on the target group.

The National Heat Fund Foundation provides loans to homeowners for substantial energy-saving measures, such as solar panels, heat pump, HR glass and insulating walls, floor and roof.The aim is to have provided 6.4 billion euros in loans by 2030. In other words: the financing of 830,000 energy-saving measures for 500,000 households and educational institutions. The financing possibilities of the National Heat Fund have been expanded in several ways since the end of 2022: • Homeowners without loan space. For this group, consumer financing of up to 10,000 euros is available at zero percent interest. For the first five years, the homeowner does not pay any repayment, after which a reassessment is carried out. • Low-income and low-middle-income homeowners. They can borrow at an interest rate of 0%. • The funding possibilities have been extended to small VvEs with less than eight apartment rights. VvEs receive an interest rate discount. For homeowners with a low or middle income, the interest rate at the Warmtefonds for the entire term is zero percent and there are no closing costs. The National Heat Fund puts the money in a building depot, so that the installer or contractor is then paid. Homeowners repay the financing in seven, ten or twenty years. In the case of interest-free financing, the amount that people repay monthly is usually less than the savings on the energy bill. Especially in combination with the national subsidy through the ISDE and the municipal subsidy (local isolation approach). The National Heat Fund is available for all homeowners, including those who are not eligible for a loan from the bank on the basis of their income or age. National Heat Fund and RVO are working on a pilot in which homeowners who apply for a loan also receive the offer to have the ISDE arranged by the Heat Fund.
Since January 2024, the Mortgage Loan Standards (Temporary Mortgage Credit Regulation) have made it possible to include additional borrowing space to make the home more sustainable.

measure_name: Improving the provision of information on financing options for sustainability
description: The government writes a guide for municipalities on how they can offer homeowners support in the financial aspects of sustainability. The Dutch government is investigating the integration of sustainability in mortgage software. The aim is to support advisors in providing financial advice on the investment needed to become more sustainable. It is desirable that they can easily see in their software package which financial options exist and financing options for sustainability (including through subsidies, the National Heat Fund, consumer and mortgage credit) are discussed as standard in advisory meetings. This research is ongoing and initial results are positive. Possibly actual implementation will take place in early 2026.

measure_name: The Standard for home insulation and target values
description: On 23 June 2021, the government published the Standard for residential insulation and the target values for building elements. The Standard originated from the Climate Agreement and was drawn up by a committee consisting of a broad representation of interested parties, such as the Association of Dutch Municipalities (VNG), Bouwend Nederland, Techniek Nederland and the Woonbond. The Standard indicates when a home is future-proof insulated and ready for a sustainable heat solution. The Standard is largely insulated, but this is possible with measures within the existing construction. When setting the standard, the feasibility of measures in an existing building has therefore been taken into account. The number of the Standard indicates the net heat demand of a house in kWh/m²/year) according to a calculation with the NTA-8800. The height of the standard is determined with a formula, which differs for 4 categories: pre-war and post-war combined with housing type multi-family or single-family. In addition, the ratio of the surface of the house and the surface of facades and roof (Als) also determines the height of the standard. The starting point is that post-war homes that meet the standard are suitable for heating with low temperature release (50 degrees supply) and pre-war suitable for MT heat supply (70 degrees supply). Agreements have already been made with the housing corporations about homes that need to be insulated, so that the average heat demand of the housing stock decreases. The standard is the reference value. See the section on the National Performance Agreements (NPA) under the heading Rental Homes below.

In the Netherlands, approximately 1.4 million owner-occupied and rental homes are covered by a VvE. This represents 18% of the total number of homes. Many non-residential functions, such as shops, are also in a VvE. If an apartment owner wants to invest in a more energy-efficient apartment, for example to reduce the energy bill, that is not easy, because apartment owners usually have to arrange that together. The Acceleration Agenda for making VvEs more sustainable sets out plans to help VvEs become more sustainable58.

In order to simplify the decision-making process of VvEs, the government intends59 to amend the Civil Code. The government programme has confirmed that decision-making on sustainability measures will be simplified. The legislative amendment means that a majority of 50% +1 of the votes is sufficient for a decision to be taken on sustainability measures and maintenance measures. And that there is no longer a mandatory attendance requirement (quorum) for a VvE decision is. The draft legislative proposal for a simpler decision-making within VvEs will be submitted for internet consultation at the end of 2025. VvEs can already get started and fortunately this is also happening more and more often. But in order to accelerate, VvEs ask for more information and guidance. That is why several initiatives have been launched for VvEs.

Unburdening VvEs involves making funds available for activation, construction and process guidance for sustainability and drawing up multi-annual maintenance plans of VvEs. In the Multi-annual Programme Climate Fund 2024, 25 million euros were allocated for a national plan of action to make the 1.2 million homes in Associations of Owners (VvEs) in the Netherlands more sustainable. First of all, efforts are being made to activate and unburden VvEs (particularly small ones). Activation is done on the one hand by encouraging VvEs to become more sustainable in laws and regulations and on the other hand with help in physical and digital form in setting up the organisation of the VvE.

measure_name: Milieu Centraal opens national knowledge centre to make VvEs more sustainable
description: Since December 2024, Milieu Centraal has been supporting municipalities and market parties with a new knowledge centre that focuses on making VvEs more sustainable, using the available knowledge at national level to strengthen local sustainability. In 2025, apartment owners who want to get started with their VvE can also contact this knowledge centre themselves for first practical support, advice and tools. Start of training Utrecht University of Applied Sciences process supervisors on making VvEs more sustainable Utrecht University of Applied Sciences has started training process supervisors who guide VvEs during the sustainability process. These professionals play a crucial role by helping to organize sustainability on behalf of the apartment owners. The training is linked to the register ‘Process supervisor for sustainability (VvE)’ at the Sertum Institute. This ensures professionalism and quality.

measure_name: Improving the financial possibilities of VvEs
description: Improving financial support for VvEs is an important part of the VvE Acceleration Agenda. It starts with the creation of a plan and for that, more subsidy is available from the Subsidy Scheme for Sustainability for Owners' Associations (SVVE). There are several subsidies for implementing energy-saving measures: • The SVVE is not only for advice, but also for the implementation of the measures. • For mixed VvEs (i.e. with private buyers and landlords), there is the incentive scheme for natural gas- free rental housing (SAH). • If apartment owners start using energy-saving measures on non-collective buildings (sometimes window frames and glass, for example, are individually owned) they are eligible for ISDE. • In addition, in the local approach of the National Insulation Programme, municipalities can also use resources to combat energy poverty and to isolate homes of owner-occupiers with poor labels to help VvEs become more sustainable. The VvEs acceleration agenda sets out the ambition to improve borrowing opportunities. For example, the application procedure at the National Heat Fund has been improved and VvEs receive an interest discount. In recent years, we have seen an increase in the number of VvEs that borrow. It is then the legal entity VvE that takes out the loan. The VvE pays repayment and interest to the financier, such as Nationaal Warmtefonds or Svn. The apartment owners do not take out a personal loan themselves. When selling the apartment there is no hassle. In fact, when sold, the apartment is more attractive, because these VvEs are seriously involved in maintenance and sustainability. The incomes of the members of the VvE do not play a role in this lending. It may happen that some apartment owners have difficulty paying the increase in the monthly VvE contribution, if it is increased by the VvE in connection with the loan. National Heat Fund is currently preparing a scheme for these owners. The idea is that individual VvE members, after checking their income and expenses, can be eligible for a financial contribution during the first years of the VvE energy savings loan. The National Heat Fund is expected to start this scheme in the second half of 2025. Another development is that SVn started the Future-proof Maintenance Fund for VvEs, which provides financial support for necessary and overdue maintenance and sustainability for VvEs from eight apartments onwards. In the case of mixed VvEs, consisting of a mix of private and professional landlords such as housing corporations and investors, the renting parties also have the possibility to repay their share of the investment directly on the loan, so that they have no obligations and liabilities towards the fund afterwards. The Future-proof Maintenance Fund for Owners’ Associations is available everywhere in the Netherlands. Specifically for small CoEs (<8 apartments), there is already an arrangement for the situation where one member cannot fulfil his/her obligations at any time. One possibility is that after a review of the financial situation of this member, the Warmtefonds will (temporarily) reduce the monthly charge for the VvE by the amount that the non-sustainable VvE member should have paid.

measure_name: Sustainability subsidy scheme for owners' associations (SVVE)
description: The sustainability subsidy scheme for owners' associations (SVVE) is a subsidy for (mixed) Owners' Associations (VvE), housing associations or housing cooperatives to make their building more sustainable. This can be done, for example, by taking energy-saving measures or purchasing a heat pump. The budget of the Sustainable Development Grant Scheme for Owners' Associations (SVVE) for the period 2023 to 2027 is €76.1 million. This total subsidy budget is for both sustainability measures and sustainability advice and research. The SVVE applies fixed amounts per m2 or per unit per sustainability measure. As with ISDE, an average percentage of 15% of the insulation costs applies to one measure, and an average subsidy of 30% applies to two or more measures. As of 1 January 2025, the SVVE has been amended on a number of aspects. For example, the maximum subsidy for advice and process guidance has been increased and the subsidy possibilities for advice, research and (construction) guidance have been expanded.

The Netherlands has approximately 3.4 million rental homes: approximately 2.3 corporation rental homes and approximately 1.1 million rental homes from private landlords. This represents about 40% of the total housing stock. Most low-income people live in rental housing. Sustainability in the rental sector has an important challenge and that is the so-called split incentive. This means that the direct benefits of the investment by the landlord (largely) benefit the tenant in the form of a lower energy bill.
In action line 2 of the NIP, the objective is to have 1 million rental homes isolated to the Standard by landlords before 2030.

measure_name: Subsidy Scheme for Sustainability and Maintenance of Rental Homes (SVOH)
description: The Subsidy Scheme for Sustainability and Maintenance of Rental Homes (SVOH) offers private landlords and institutional investors the opportunity to apply for subsidies for energy-saving measures, maintenance measures and energy advice for their rental homes. The SVOH scheme runs from April 2022 to December 2029 and can - as of 1 April 2023 - be used by all private landlords, other than housing corporations. The SVOH scheme has a budget of 152 million euros. Partly this is also compensation for loss of income as a result of the rent freeze of 1 July 2021. In order to maintain the investment capacity of landlords, the SVOH is made available as a contribution to this. The subsidy applies to one or more energy-saving measures. When applying for one energy saving measure, the subsidy amount is reduced by half. There is also a bonus per m2 per insulation measure for the use of sustainable insulation materials. Maintenance measures are only eligible if at least an energy-saving measure is taken, such as new frames or a ventilation system. The SVOH also provides a 75% subsidy on the costs of having an energy advice drawn up. For the energy advice, at least one energy saving measure must also be implemented in order to be eligible for this subsidy. In all cases, the subsidy amounts to a maximum of 10,000 euros per home, without a maximum per landlord. If a landlord installs a solar boiler or heat pump in addition to an energy-saving measure, there is a max of 15,000 euros per home. For monumental rental properties, different conditions and amounts apply. For example, a monument can also apply for a subsidy for HR glass.

measure_name: Support package to make private landlords more sustainable
description: In March 2025, a support package on making private landlords more sustainable was published. The support package consists of four components, namely: 1) improving information provision and process support, 2) strengthening cooperation with local and regional authorities and industry; 3) improving financial support (see also heading ‘Financing opportunities for private landlords’) and 4) phasing out worst insulated rental homes by regulation.

The investment space for private landlords has been reduced by recent fiscal measures. Private landlords can use the SVOH but not the National Heat Fund. That is why, together with mortgage lenders, we are investigating whether more attractive lending opportunities for private landlords can be offered by market parties.

measure_name: Phasing out EGF energy labels for rental housing by 2029
description: Landlords will be required to phase out EGF energy labels on rental homes by 2029. For this purpose, minimum energy performance requirements for rental homes are included in the Decree on Buildings and the Living Environment (Bbl). In order not to impose unfeasible and unnecessary requirements, a number of exceptions are used. Examples of exceptions are monuments, houses that are used for a maximum of two years, houses that are used for less than 4 months per year and detached houses smaller than 50m2. The scheme in the Bbl will enter into force on 1 January 2029. In line with these proposed regulations with regard to minimum energy performance requirements, the government intends to extend the line to 2040, from then on rental homes must at least meet an energy label B. There will be no rental ban for rental homes in the regulations. Landlords can continue to rent out the house, but there will be requirements that require them to reduce the energy demand of the house. Landlords will have until 1 January 2029 to address the rental properties with the EGF labels. If they do not do so, the municipality in question can maintain from 1 January 2029 to ensure that landlords improve the rental property to at least label D. In doing so, the municipality will have existing enforcement tools, such as the possibility of writing down landlords, possibly subject to a penalty payment.

On 30 June 2022, the Minister for VRO made national performance agreements with Aedes, Woonbond and VNG. The agreements were reconsidered in 2024. The ambition for a natural gas-free housing stock in 2050 remains unchanged, but the parties set the intermediate target for 450,000 natural gas-free homes from 2030 to 2034. As a result, more steps can be taken in this period in insulating housing corporation property and in installing hybrid heat pumps. The parties have also agreed to focus more on reducing the average heat demand of rental homes. As a result, the measures with the best relationship between costs on the one hand and a reduction in heat demand on the other hand are taken first. In 2024, the average heat demand of all housing corporations will be 108 kWh/m2. The heat demand reduction path is the annual reduction of heat demand over time, plotted with an intermediate target for the average heat demand of the stock of 94 kWh/m2 in 2030 and 87 kWh/m2 in 2034. In addition, the agreement remains that housing corporations will phase out homes with poor energy labels (EFG) by 2028 at the latest.

measure_name: Modernisation of the Housing Valuation System (WWS)
description: The housing valuation system (WWS) prescribes maximum rents based on points for the quality of the home. For example for surface area, energy label and WOZ value. Since the Affordable Rent Act entered into force60 on 1 July 2024, the WWS has become mandatory. Making the WWS mandatory means that landlords are obliged to adhere to the maximum rents that match the quality of the home. Part of this law is a modernization of the WWS, so that homes with higher energy labels are better valued, while homes with lower labels receive deduction points. As a result, the sustainability of a home will play a greater role in determining the maximum rental price. This will - in addition to the standardization to improve rental homes with an energy label E, F or G to at least D from 1 January 2029 - also encourage private landlords to move towards sustainability.

On 1 October 2023, the revision of the Lease Energy Performance Compensation Decree entered into force. For certain homes, a landlord can charge an energy performance fee (EPV). These are very well insulated homes with solar panels and a heat pump that deliver a guaranteed performance. The amount of the EPV is legally capped with the Decree on Energy Performance Compensation for Rent, so that the tenant keeps the same housing costs. With the EPV, landlords get more investment opportunities when building or renovating highly energy-efficient rental homes.

This section discusses policies and measures for making Dutch non-residential buildings more sustainable. Subsidy schemes and other support programmes are discussed first, financing products for non-residential construction are explained, and standards and other relevant policy measures are discussed.

measure_name: Sustainable Social Real Estate Grant Scheme (DUMAVA)
description: The DUMAVA scheme is a subsidy scheme to help owners of social real estate meet the costs of sustainability. The scheme is intended for owners of buildings with a social function such as schools, community centres, healthcare institutions, municipal real estate and amateur sports associations. Social real estate owners can apply for up to three sustainability measures or an integrated project. Both forms can be combined with subsidies for energy advice and for drawing up an energy label after implementing the sustainability measures. Integrated projects are expected to have a level of ambition that is in line with the government's climate objectives. Owners receive additional subsidies when sustainability is achieved to a very high level of energy performance. In this way, we want to increase the pace for making social real estate more sustainable and contribute to national and European objectives, such as the renovation obligation in the Energy Efficiency Directive (Article 6). The grant scheme will be evaluated annually and, if necessary, adjusted prior to the next grant round. The evaluations show that there is a huge need for (financial) support for the sustainability task. The subsidy scheme is reopened annually. The scheme was opened for the first time in 2022. For 2022 and 2023, the subsidy scheme was financed from the Dutch Recovery and Resilience Plan. For the period 2024 to 2030, 1.9 billion euros have been made available from the Climate Fund.

In the Dutch Climate Agreement (2019), agreements were made to work towards the climate targets for 2030 and 2050. For social real estate, it has been agreed that the sectors themselves determine the route to work towards these objectives. These twelve sectors (e.g. education, care, sport, local and regional authorities) in social real estate have agreed in the proposal for the Climate Agreement that they will make sectoral roadmaps in which it is clear how their real estate will become CO2 low towards 2050. A first version of the roadmaps was made in 2019. These sectoral roadmaps are a form of self-regulation, the Ministry of VRO only has a coordinating responsibility. In January 2020, the sector organisations submitted final roadmaps or additions to the previously submitted roadmaps. The purpose of the development in different scenarios was, among other things, to provide insight into the different investment questions at different sustainability rates for budgetary purposes at the relevant ministries. These scenarios have been used to identify the financial instruments needed. The first versions of the sectoral roadmaps showed, inter alia, bottlenecks in funding. In several sectoral roadmaps, the individual institutions within the sector have started to draw up portfolio roadmaps for their real estate. In 2025, the sectoral roadmaps were updated.

The portfolio approach is a new way of working for the energy savings obligation. Companies or institutions with 20 or more buildings in the Netherlands, spread over at least 2 environmental services, are eligible for the portfolio approach. The portfolio approach offers large organisations more flexibility and less administration. In return, their real estate must deliver over-statutory energy performance, expressed in Key Performance Indicators (KPI). A participating company or institution submits the energy-saving measures of its entire real estate portfolio to one coordinating inspector (CI). Portfolio roadmaps shall be included in the enforcement strategy for competent authorities. The portfolio approach has 32 participants after the start. These commit to achieving a reduction in fossil energy use of at least 5.5% per year. This should lead to higher energy savings than required by law. The portfolio roadmap must be submitted for assessment to Omgevingsdient NL. In that roadmap, the measures to be taken to achieve the reduction target must be specified at portfolio level over a period of four years.

Many owners of non-residential buildings lack the knowledge or the capacity to make their building more sustainable. To help them, two relief programmes are aimed at the small owners within social real estate and SMEs. These programmes support owners in creating a sustainability plan for their premises and eventual business process. These programmes are implemented by the provinces and run until 2027. 62 There are also programmes from different sectors, taking into account the specific challenges in that sector, such as for sport or for monuments. The relief programme for social real estate started in 2021 and a second tranche of the scheme was opened to provinces in 2022. All 12 provinces make use of the national contribution. The objective is to provide support to 2,850 owners until May 1, 2027. More than 1550 owners are already taking part in a carefree process. There are resources to continue the relief programme until 2030. In its design, the requirements of the EPBD-IV aimed at informing and unburdening building owners61 are taken into account. In February 2024, the Dedicated Allowance Unburdening Sustainability Small and Micro SMEs and business parks were published. Here, provinces were able to apply for funds to set up two programmes: the SME Care Programme and the Sustainable Business Areas Programme. Approximately €50 million is available for both programmes. The SME Care Programme aims to support small and micro SMEs in making their lives more sustainable. The Sustainability Business Parks Programme is aimed at increasing the degree of organisation on business parks for the purpose of sustainability. The application has been accepted from all provinces. On 1 May, the provinces started implementing both programmes, which run until 1 May 2027 with the aim of helping a total of 5700 SMEs and 650 business parks to become more sustainable. The funds for both programmes are available for guidance and advice, not for the financing of the measures themselves. Each province gives its own interpretation to the programmes and makes the choice itself which small SMEs and business parks they can unburden within the programme.

measure_name: Knowledge and Innovation Platform Sustainability Social Real Estate
description: The Knowledge and Innovation Platform for Sustainable Social Real Estate (KIP-MV) was established in 2019 to support the sustainability of buildings in the social sector. The platform stimulates energy savings, improving energy performance and the use of sustainable energy from social real estate and promotes innovation. The platform does this by developing and disseminating knowledge. Within the KIP-MV, knowledge parties from the healthcare, sports, monuments, museums, education and municipalities join forces and exchange information, examples, knowledge and innovations. The two objectives of the Platform are: - Achieving demand and knowledge articulation with regard to the sustainability of social real estate - Collaboration and synergy between sectors.

In order to bring forward investments in the sustainability of buildings and installations, appropriate financing is desirable. We are currently working on low-threshold loans for making social real estate more sustainable.62 The government is making a contribution to the National Renovation Fund, the BNG Sustainability Fund and the Regional Energy Funds. In order to promote access to finance for integrated projects and area-oriented solutions linked to social real estate, a social real estate guarantee fund is being developed. Through Qredits, SMEs have access to easily accessible and attractive loans of up to € 50,000 to make energy use more sustainable (see SME Sustainability Loan on www.qredits.nl).

measure_name: The Schools Energy Savings Loan of the National Heat Fund
description: In 2019, Stichting Nationaal Warmtefonds started a pilot with loans for making PO and VO schools more sustainable. In the period 2019 to 2022, loans were granted to around twenty schools for a total of more than 2.5 million euros. No loans have been granted to schools since 2023. If a new application is received, Warmtefonds will process it. The Schools Energy Savings Loan can be used for facade insulation, cavity wall insulation, roof insulation, solar panels, LED lighting and energy management systems.

Invest-NL has carried out research into how the threshold for financing energy-saving measures for SMEs can be removed. The study shows that the costs of the mandatory energy-saving measures amount to approximately € 16,500 per company. Due to this relatively small financing need, and a lack of collateral, it is challenging for SMEs to find financing with an affordable interest rate. About 11% of SMEs indicate that they do not have access to external financing before or now. Combined with CBS data, this indicates a total of around 11,000 SMEs. To remove this threshold, InvestNL proposes an Energy Savings Fund to support SMEs by providing loans for both mandatory and other energy-saving measures. By linking uniform conditions to the loans and using the arithmetic interest rate for the energy savings obligation, SMEs throughout the Netherlands would then have access to – and certainty about – external financing, the interest costs of which correspond to the arithmetic interest rate used when determining the payback period for the energy savings obligation. Within the Climate Fund, € 150 million has been earmarked to support SMEs in energy saving. Of this, € 100 million has been earmarked for a possible energy savings fund. The government takes the results of InvestNL's research into the decision-making on the use of the funds. For the remaining € 50 million, an unburdening programme for sustainability in general for energy-intensive SMEs (€ 25 million) and financing of sustainability loans for small SMEs through Qredits (€ 25 million, of which € 10 million has already been granted). The relief programme supports SMEs with advice and implementation of sustainability measures. Qredits provides cheap sustainability loans to entrepreneurs who are not subject to the energy savings obligation.

The Netherlands has already included requirements for the energy performance of new buildings in the building regulations, the so-called NZEB standard (Almost Energy Neutral Buildings). The Netherlands has not yet included any requirements for existing buildings. Chapter 5 discusses how the Netherlands will determine the requirements and limit values for Zero Emission Buildings (ZEB). Member States have the possibility to set different limit values for existing buildings than for new buildings. By including this standard in the Bbl, all parties have clarity about what the building stock must meet in 2050. These standards apply to the entire non- residential building and are not yet mandatory. Until the new ZEB limit values have been set, the renovation standard for non-residential buildings will be applied. The renovation standard (energy label A++ or A+++) is an existing, voluntary guideline for the desired energy performance of a building in 2050. This renovation standard is already being stimulated through existing instruments, for example because renovations to this standard receive a higher percentage of subsidy within the DUMAVA.63

As part of the implementation of the EPBD IV, the Netherlands will introduce new minimum energy performance requirements for non-residential buildings. See also Chapter 6. Since 1 January 2023, every office building in the Netherlands must already have a minimum energy label C.64 If the building does not meet the requirements, it may no longer be used as an office. The energy label C obligation shall not apply where:

measure_name: Energy savings objectives stemming from the EED Directive Articles 5 and 6
description: The renewed Energy Efficiency Directive (EDD) requires Member States to reduce energy consumption. Public authorities should play an exemplary role in this regard. The EED imposes obligations on Member States to reduce the energy use of public bodies (Article 5) and to achieve the sustainability of public bodies’ buildings (Article 6). Article 6 states that 3% of the total floor area of heated and/or cooled buildings with a floor area larger than 250 m2 owned by public bodies must be renovated annually into nearly zero-energy buildings or zero-emission buildings. Until the ZEB standard for existing construction has been established, the renovation standard for non- residential buildings will be applied. The renovation standard corresponds to energy label A++ or A+++ (depending on the use function of a building education, sports, shop, office, etc.) which goes hand in hand with low energy consumption. It is a voluntary standard for the desired energy performance of a building in 2050. Energy saving obligation and recognised lists of measures (EML) An energy saving obligation has been included in the Environmental Management Act since 1993. The energy saving obligation is a legal obligation for companies and institutions that consume more than 50,000 kWh of electricity or 25,000 m³ of natural gas annually. They must implement all energy-saving measures with a payback period of up to five years, including measures that reduce CO₂ emissions. The recognised list of measures (EML) was updated for the second round in 2023. The update unlocks greater savings potential because more savings measures meet the five-year payback period, including the hybrid heat pump. It is therefore mandatory since 1 July 2023 for companies and organisations where a hybrid heat pump earns itself back within 5 years at an independent moment to install a hybrid heat pump. The government has decided to tighten the energy saving obligation by increasing the payback period to seven years in 2027. The competent authority (the ILT and SodM, provinces and municipalities and the regional implementation and environmental services mandated by them) is responsible for monitoring and enforcing the energy savings obligation.

measure_name: Addressing renewable energy sources in and on buildings
Solar PV: preferably on roofs and facades
description: With the tightening of the preferential solar order, as agreed administratively in October 2023 between the government, Interprovincial Consultation (IPO), Association of Dutch Municipalities (VNG), the Union of Water Boards (UvW) and Netbeheer Nederland (NBNL), the Netherlands puts on solar PV according to the steps of the preferential solar order:

The government is filling in the mandatory exemplary role of public buildings for the generation of renewable energy through, among other things, the programme Zon op Rijksdaken. The government is implementing the administrative agreements to use 80 percent of the suitable government roofs in 2030 for a second function, such as the generation of renewable energy, through, among other things, the program Zon op Rijksdaken of the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf. Roofs are considered suitable when investing with solar panels is technically feasible. In the meantime, an inventory has been made of how many roofs – national offices and defence buildings – will be equipped with solar PV by the end of 2025. In addition, twelve of the 70 national offices with suitable roofs have already been invested with solar panels and fourteen additional roofs are being invested. This is the estimate that about 37 percent of the suitable office roofs are used. With regard to the defence real estate, 96 of the 540 buildings with a suitable roof are used (approximately 18 percent). The Sun-on-Rijksdaken programme will expire on 31 December 2025. The EPBD replaces the Zon-Op-Rijksdaken programme for the installation of solar panels on government buildings. Depending on the building size, the obligation to install solar panels will be elaborated in regulations from 2027, in accordance with the EPBD.

The EPBD IV lays down rules on mandatory installation of a solar energy system where this is technically, functionally and economically feasible. The Netherlands will implement this by requiring a solar energy installation for the generation of building-related energy consumption. For new non-residential buildings with a surface area of more than 250 m2, these rules shall apply by 31 December 2026. For existing public buildings, a gradual approach is foreseen whereby buildings larger than 2,000 m2 of use area must comply with the new rules by 31 December 2027. This threshold will be progressively reduced to 250 m2 by December 2030. Existing non-residential buildings larger than 500 m2 will be subject to the obligation from 31 December 2027, when they undergo major renovation. For new residential buildings and new covered parking garages, the rules apply from 31 December 2029.

The bill terminating the netting scheme was adopted by the Senate on 17 December 2024. With this important legislative change, the netting scheme will be terminated as of 2027, and every active customer will receive a reasonable fee for returned renewable electricity, in accordance with the agreement from the Mainline Agreement and the Government Programme. In the period between now and 2027, the preparation for the careful implementation of this law will be taken up in consultation with the parties involved. Terminating the netting scheme creates a financial incentive for active customers to use renewable electricity more efficiently. By using self-generated electricity, the entire supply rate is saved, and no VAT and energy tax is due. In the coming years, more attention will be paid to the knowledge and possibilities that households have to use the electricity generated by themselves as efficiently as possible in the home. After all, this is in the interest of both a shorter payback period for solar panels and a reduction in the load on the electricity grid.

In making the built environment more sustainable, the goal is to achieve 1 million installed hybrid heat pumps in the existing building by 2030. According to PBL's updated start-up analysis, two thirds of homes will eventually be heated by a hybrid heat pump (using sustainable gas) or fully electric heat pump by 2050.66 With an electric heat pump you no longer use natural gas and with a hybrid heat pump you use about 60% less natural gas for space heating. It is therefore important to have the preconditions for this technique in order and to provide support where necessary. In addition, based on the EPBD-IV Article 13.7, Member States are encouraged to replace fossil fuel boilers in existing buildings and to make national plans for the phase-out of such boilers by 2040. The new government intends to stimulate and standardise the application of hybrid, smart heat pumps by 2029, where heat networks do not offer a suitable solution. Below we will discuss the ways in which the heat pump is stimulated as an alternative to the central heating boiler for different target groups. The action plan on hybrid heat pumps, the promotion and financing of heat pumps, the hybrid heat pump as a measure in the energy saving obligation, the information campaign aimed at heat pumps and the network-friendly integration of heat pumps are discussed in turn.

The Action Plan on Hybrid Heat Pumps 2022-2024 was published on 15 June 202267. In this Action Plan, agreements have been made with the most important sector parties such as the installers and producers. The aim was to achieve a substantial scale-up of hybrid heat pumps in the short term. In addition to scaling up production and the availability of sustainable installations, the agreements were about reducing manufacturing costs, shortening installation time, unambiguous monitoring of, among other things, the number of heat pumps, communication, knowledge and insight into performance and additional stimulation. The Action Plan has contributed to the significant expansion of production capacity in the Netherlands in recent years through the creation of new factories and production lines. The installation of heat pumps has also taken off. Furthermore, the installation time for hybrid heat pumps has been reduced. In addition, the demo project hybrid heat pumps and the installation monitor provided valuable information about the performance of the (hybrid) heat pump and its impact on the electricity grid. From within the government, we have managed to accommodate the growing number of applications in the ISDE, we have conducted various government campaigns and from 2025, with the help of CBS, we will shape the monitoring even better. Because it is 66 Update Start-up analysis of natural gas-free neighbourhoods 2025 | Planning Bureau for the Environment important that the right heat pump is installed in the specific occupant situation, the approach will be continued and broadened to all types of heat pumps, both hybrid and fully electric, from 2025 onwards, and the framework conditions such as a grid-friendly integration will be looked at more broadly. Up to 2023, around 560,000 heat pumps have been sold, the vast majority of which are fully electric heat pumps. To achieve the goal of 1 million hybrid heat pumps by 2030, growth will have to accelerate.

measure_name: Promotion and financing of heat pumps
description: Consumers often opt for a new boiler when the old one needs to be replaced. This reluctance is partly due to the unfamiliarity of the technology and its energy-saving possibilities, but the initial investment, which is higher than a traditional central heating boiler, is also perceived as an important threshold. To encourage residents to make the switch to a (hybrid) heat pump, the government therefore makes Investment subsidy for sustainable energy (ISDE) available for the switch to a heat pump. This subsidy covers on average 30% of the investment costs. This helps the citizen with the investment and makes the switch more attractive. In addition, residents can use a loan at attractive conditions with the National Heat Fund. Residents with an aggregate income below € 60,000 do not have to pay interest on this. This also allows people with a lower income to benefit from the benefits of a heat pump. There may also be further support at the local level. Information about this can be found on the Energy subsidy guide of Milieu Centraal, where you can search for local subsidy and loan possibilities per place of residence.

measure_name: Heat pumps in the energy saving obligation for companies and institutions
description: The energy saving obligation obliges companies and institutions to implement all energy saving measures - with a payback period of 5 years or less. The recognised list of measures used in the Energy Savings Obligation also includes the hybrid heat pump measure. It is therefore mandatory since 1 July 2023 for companies and institutions where a hybrid heat pump earns itself back within 5 years at an independent moment to install a hybrid heat pump.

Residents and SMEs have recently been made aware of the benefits of a hybrid heat pump through a government campaign under the banner of Zet. This campaign focused on residents and SMEs who move, renovate or whose boiler needs to be replaced. There was targeted use via magazines, information on websites, radio spots and cooperation with a mortgage lender. On the website of Milieu Centraal, residents and entrepreneurs can find reliable and accessible information about heat pumps. In addition, residents can get information via the improvement check on the website verbeterjehuis.nl about the concrete steps they can take for their own home to become more sustainable and what savings that leads to.

measure_name: Prerequisite: Net-friendly integration of heat pumps
description: The space on the electricity grid is an important precondition for the growth of the number of heat pumps. Increasing electrification means that the electricity grids are becoming increasingly full. The impact of heat pumps on the low-voltage grid can be reduced by using heat pumps more flexibly. In that case, for example, a heat pump can make more use of its own generation by solar panels. The heat pump can also start earlier or at a lower power during the evening peak on the electricity grid. In this way, the grid load of a heat pump can be reduced without loss of comfort. The Action Agenda on network congestion for low-voltage grids agreed that smart devices – including smart heat pumps – should become the norm. In order to reach agreements that smart heat pumps must meet, the Royal Dutch Standards Institute (NEN) has been commissioned to develop a Dutch Technical Agreement (NTA) for smart heat pumps. The results of the standard trajectory are expected in early 2026. Once the NTA has been developed, the results can be used, for example, for a link to laws and regulations, or the ISDE. In this way, the installation of smart heat pumps can be stimulated.

In a climate-neutral Netherlands, part of the energy supply will still run on gas. However, this is not natural gas, but gas that is completely free of greenhouse gas emissions, such as green gas. For this, it is necessary that green gas production grows exponentially from around 0.3 billion m3 (bcm; billion cubic metres) in 2022 to the policy target of 2 bcm. The Green Gas Programme, the blending obligation for green gas and subsidy schemes contribute to achieving this goal. For the built environment, green gas is limited available and always in combination with a hybrid heat pump.

This Programme concerns the scaling up of green gas production in the Netherlands to at least 2 bcm of green gas. This ambition is supported by measures in the areas of 1) business case, 2) spatial integration and 3) raw materials. In 2024, there was a small stagnation, and green gas production grew by only 5% from 282 million cubic metres of green gas to 294 million cubic metres of green gas. The green gas sector indicates to be optimistic about the coming years by expecting the announced government policy and further growth towards the set targets for the production and blending of green gas.

In 2025, work will continue on the green gas blending obligation. Under this bill, energy suppliers who supply gas are given an administrative obligation to achieve a certain amount of chain emission reduction annually through the supply of green gas, increasing to a total of 2.85 Mton CO2 eq. in 2031. The level per supplier shall be determined on the basis of the share per supplier in the total supply of natural gas to the end-user group. Green gas is supplied via the existing natural gas network. This is an administrative obligation, because it is not possible to physically measure how much green gas has been supplied to the end-user group. In order to demonstrate administratively that an energy supplier complies with the obligation, the existing Guarantees of Origin (GvOs) are used and new marketable units are used, namely the green gas unit (GGE). The Dutch Emissions Authority (NEa), which is the proposed executive and supervisory body, determines annually how many GGEs an energy supplier must surrender in order to comply with the obligation. The NEa is also responsible for the implementation of ETS2. Partly because of implementation reasons, the execution was searched as much as possible for coincidence with ETS2, the share of the built environment in this end-user group is about 70%. In May 2024, the proposal for a blending obligation was presented to the Council of State and the European Commission for advice and notification as a technical regulation, respectively. The Commission responded to this notification with a detailed opinion, focusing on the condition that only green gas produced from a production plant located in the Netherlands can count towards the blending obligation. This requirement is considered by the Commission in the UGM as an unjustified infringement of the free movement of goods, as it is under the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. As a result, the bill will be amended so that green gas produced in other Member States and introduced into the European gas network can also contribute to the blending obligation. The Chamber was further informed about this in July 2025. After consulting the Council of State on the bill (end of 2025 - beginning of 2026), the parliamentary examination of the bill can begin in 2026.

Since 2020, the previous sustainable energy production (SDE+) scheme has been broadened to the Sustainable Energy Transition (SDE++) incentive scheme. This scheme stimulates the deployment of renewable energy and CO2 reducing techniques by remunerating the unprofitable top of these techniques by means of an operating subsidy. In principle, this also applies to greenhouse gases other than CO2, such as methane. The SDE++ makes the business case of emission reduction measures more attractive, and thus increases the investment willingness of companies. In 2023, so-called "fences" were introduced within the SDE++. These are flexible reservations in the domains of Low Temperature Heat, High Temperature Heat and Molecules, which must ensure that techniques that are less cost-effective in the short term, but necessary for the energy transition, are covered more.

measure_name: Promoting smart technologies and charging infrastructure for sustainable mobility in buildings
Recharging infrastructure obligations in and near buildings
description: Since 10 March 2020, the following obligations for charging infrastructure for buildings have been laid down in the Decree on Buildings in the Living Environment (Bbl), which enshrines rules on buildings in the physical living environment:68 • For new residential buildings and existing residential buildings undergoing major renovation, with more than 10 parking spaces on the building plot, pipe infrastructure (free pipes) must be constructed for each parking space to construct recharging points. • For new non-residential buildings and for existing non-residential buildings undergoing major renovation, with more than 10 parking spaces on the same site, a minimum of 1 charging point for the entire parking space must be constructed. Pipe infrastructure (free pipes) must also be built for 1 in 5 parking spaces. For existing non-residential buildings with more than 20 parking spaces on the site, a minimum of 1 charging point must be installed from 1 January 2025. The EPBD IV contains agreements on the requirements that future parking spaces must meet. These are processed in the Bbl in due course. The proposed amendments to the Bbl have recently been consulted and are expected to enter into force in 2026:69 For new or substantially renovated housing with more than 3 parking spaces, wiring pipes must be installed to all parking spaces. Also, 50% of parking spaces must have pre-cabling to place charging points. At least one charging point shall be installed. Finally, the building has at least 2 parking spaces for bicycles for each residential unit. For new or substantially renovated non-residential construction , with more than 5 parking spaces, the following requirements shall be met: • All parking spaces have cables for charging infrastructure. • At least 50% of all parking spaces have pre-cabling to place charging points. • At least 20% of all parking spaces have a charging point. Is the building an office? Then at least 50% of all parking spaces have a charging point. • The building has bicycle parking spaces for at least 10% of the maximum, or 15% of the average user capacity of the building. For existing non-residential buildings with more than 20 parking spaces, one of the following rules must be complied with: • At least 50% of all parking spaces have wiring lines, or • At least 10% of all parking spaces have a charging point. • Is the building owned or used by a public authority? In that case, at least 50% of all parking spaces will have pre-cabling to place charging points by 1 January 2033. • The building has bicycle parking spaces for at least 10% of the maximum, or 15% of the average user capacity of the building.

measure_name: Measures to stimulate charging infrastructure at VvE complexes
description: Currently, permission from the VvE is required for the installation of a charging point at a VvE complex. New legislation is being prepared to ease decision-making on this issue. Under the bill on the notification scheme for VvE charging points, an apartment owner can suffice with a notification (notification) to the VvE board when installing a charging point, if a number of conditions are met. The bill was in internet consultation from 12 July 2021 to 6 September 202170 and is now being taken forward. Expanding the right of initiative for tenants of living space with charging points in the context of removing obstacles is also part of the bill. Other activities in the area of stimulating infrastructure for sustainable mobility within VvE complexes focus on subsidies or the provision of information. For example, within the Subsidy Scheme for Sustainability for Owners' Associations (SVVE), a subsidy is provided for a charging point advice, in which it is advised how the VvE realizes charging points on its own parking space in a future-proof way, and for basic charging infrastructure, so that residents can place charging points.71 In addition, the website www.vveladen.nl provides information to VvEs and VvE members about the construction of VvE charging infrastructure or the expansion of existing charging points.

measure_name: Measures to stimulate charging infrastructure in non-residential buildings
description: Entrepreneurs can apply for a subsidy to build charging infrastructure and receive advice, from the SPRILA advice and SPRILA Acquisition schemes. The Subsidy Scheme for Private Charging Infrastructure at Companies (SPRILA) Advice is available for entrepreneurs who want advice on the construction of charging infrastructure for electric vehicles on their own or rented land. The amount of the subsidy is 50% of the total costs, up to a maximum of € 3,500. A total of €500,000 will be available for this scheme in 2025.72 The Subsidy Scheme for Private Charging Infrastructure at Companies (SPRILA) Purchase for charging infrastructure for own vehicles or vehicles of employees, customers or suppliers subsidises the costs for the charging infrastructure for electric vehicles and their construction. This concerns charging infrastructure that is placed on the entrepreneur's own or rented premises, which is not always publicly accessible. In combination with charging infrastructure, a subsidy can be requested for a stationary battery under certain conditions. In 2025, a total of € 60,952,000 will be available for this scheme.73

measure_name: Combating and preventing energy poverty through energy saving and sustainability
description: Saving energy and making homes more sustainable is the most important way to contribute to an affordable energy bill for residents with a small stock exchange. The government is continuing the phase-out of rental housing with energy labels E, F and G (see 3.1.2, under rental housing). This objective is laid down in the renewed National Performance Agreements (2024) with housing corporations and municipalities. On the contrary, this is also relevant because about two thirds (62% in 2022 and 66% in 2023) of energy-poor households lived in corporate housing (TNO, 2024). Households are further supported through the National Insulation Programme (NIP), the National Heat Fund and the Schemes for the Promotion of Natural Gas-Free Rental (Stimulation Scheme for Natural Gas-Free Rental Homes (SAH) and for Owners' Associations (Sustainability Scheme for Owners' Associations (SVVE)). These instruments are described in section 3.1.

measure_name: Municipal resources to tackle energy poverty
description: Municipalities received a total of €550 million in three instalments in 2022 and 2023 to address energy poverty through the SPUK Approach to Energy Poverty. Municipalities have been given a lot of space to deploy the funds until the end of 2025, for example so that they can quickly strengthen an existing local approach. Many municipalities opt for the use of energy fixers and coaches and white goods schemes. Studies (TNO, AMS Institute) show that the deployment of energy aid organisations can lead to significant energy savings. The implementation period of this SPUK will be extended from 2025 to 2027 so that municipalities have more time for implementation.

In 2025, 56.3 million was made available to the Temporary Emergency Energy Fund Foundation to set up an energy fund that provides support to low-income households with a high energy bill, to prevent debts from arising or possibly a forced closure of energy.
